report: No power analyses were detected.

::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

text.text: Background: Asthma is a chronic, multifactorial disease that progresses in episodes and requires effective coordination of care between healthcare professionals and patients.
Objective: To describe and evaluate pre-hospital therapeutic management of asthma attacks.

Methods: Cross-sectional, prospective, single-centre, observational and descriptive study of patients consulting for asthma attacks at the Fort de France paediatric emergency department between July and November 2024.
All patients included were children between the ages of 1 and 18 who had already been diagnosed with asthma by a doctor and who presented to the emergency department for an asthma attack.

Several other parameters were assessed, such as the parents' perception of the emergency situation, the child's asthma control in the month prior to the attack, the child's usual medical follow-up, and their usual treatment.
Results: 175 patients were included in the study.
Eight patients were excluded from the study because their questionnaire had a response rate of less than 50%.

Of the 175 patients included, only 6.7% received perfect pre-hospital care, 29.3% received good quality care, 36% received moderate quality care, and 10.3% received poor quality care before arriving at the emergency department.
(17.7% did not complete all the items necessary to calculate the score).
11.6% of children did not receive treatment before consulting the emergency department.
Among the 88.9% who took short-acting β2 agonists, only 52% received at least 3 series and 66.2% were given doses appropriate for their weight.
21.6% received oral corticosteroids before arriving at the emergency department.
The management of asthma attacks outside of hospital settings is not optimal for a large proportion of patients in the study.
Several areas for improvement have been identified and require joint action by healthcare professionals.
Asthma is a chronic respiratory disease with a high prevalence in the paediatric population.

According to the World Health Organization (WHO), there are currently an estimated 262 million patients with asthma, and the estimated number of asthma-related deaths worldwide is 455,000 per year. (1) In France, asthma affects 4 million people and it is estimated that 10 to 12% of the population will have asthma during their lifetime.

The prevalence of asthma in children in the French West Indies is estimated at 15 to 20%, compared with 10 to 12% for children in mainland France, all regions combined. (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?ChfmT3) This difference has not yet been clearly explained, although several hypotheses have been put forward, including higher humidity levels conducive to mould growth and the sandstorm phenomenon, which is well known in the Caribbean.

text.text: Asthma is a chronic inflammatory respiratory disease that manifests itself in attacks of varying intensity, which may resolve spontaneously or lead to severe respiratory distress and even death.
Clinically, it is defined by a combination of several clinical signs: wheezing, dyspnoea, coughing, chest tightness and limited expiratory airflow.
The clinical presentation varies, particularly in terms of symptom intensity, depending on the attack and the individual.
The diagnosis is based primarily on the combination of symptoms presented by the patient and their progression over time.

It will be confirmed by several paraclinical tests carried out outside of attacks (respiratory function testing, peak flow, stress test), in order to make a definitive diagnosis and refine the therapeutic management.

The clinical expression of asthma is highly variable, and asthma is currently classified into different clinical-biological phenotypes: (5) • eosinophilic asthma • neutrophilic asthma • asthma with predominant cough • late-onset asthma (first symptoms in adulthood) • asthma with persistent ventilatory limitation • asthma with obesity

text.text: The factors contributing to asthma attacks are numerous, multifactorial and sometimes poorly understood.
They make it difficult for health and public health authorities to control and prevent asthma attacks in the general population.

These include allergens, irritants (such as tobacco smoke) (https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?7vVeWN air pollutants (such as fine particles), intense physical activity, climates (humid and hot), and viral respiratory infections (RSV/adenovirus, etc.).

text.text: In certain situations, several interrelated risk factors can lead to an attack, hence the importance of isolating the causative agents in order to adapt the environment and lifestyle habits of patients.

Numerous genes that may contribute to asthma have been isolatedhttps://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?D1dkcR particularly in certain regions of chromosome 17 (7) , however, this knowledge is limited to the field of research and its incorporation into clinical practice is currently limited.

text.text: There is no organised screening for asthma to date.
Asthma most often manifests itself in childhood.

It can persist into adulthood, manifest itself subclinically, or sometimes fade over time. (8) The impact on the quality of life of patients and their loved ones (particularly parents of children with asthma) is significant.

text.text: The frequency and intensity of exacerbations can lead to repeated visits to healthcare facilities. (9) Exacerbations manifest as respiratory distress, which can sometimes be severe, with symptoms that are often very noisy and anxiety-inducing for the patient and those accompanying them.

text.text: This can lead to repeated visits to emergency departments and a deterioration in quality of life in the short to medium term.

The repercussions can be long-term, as there is a close link between the severity of asthma in childhood and the risk of developing chronic obstructive pulmonary disease in adulthood. (10) To date, asthma-related morbidity remains high, and despite advances in treatment and support, asthma is a public health priority in France and around the world.

text.text: Short-acting β2 agonists (SABAs) are the cornerstone of emergency management.

Their use is standardised and the dose administered will depend on the clinical severity of the attack and the patient's weight. (11) The recommendations of the SP2A (Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology Society) define the management of moderate to severe asthma attacks as appropriate if: ❖ Administration of short-acting β2 agonists ❖ Adjusted to the patient's weight (4 to 12 puffs per series) ❖ At least 3 series administered ❖ 20-minute interval between SABA series ❖ Oral corticosteroids administered from the 3rd SABA series onwards ❖ Call the emergency number if symptoms persist and signs of severity are present The administration of SABA requires the use of an inhalation chamber with a mask (for children aged 0 to 3 years) or a mouthpiece (for children aged 4 to 12 years).
text.formatted: Their use is standardised and the dose administered will depend on the clinical severity of the attack and the patient's weight. <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(11)</ref> The recommendations of the SP2A (Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology Society) define the management of moderate to severe asthma attacks as appropriate if: ❖ Administration of short-acting β2 agonists ❖ Adjusted to the patient's weight (4 to 12 puffs per series) ❖ At least 3 series administered ❖ 20-minute interval between SABA series ❖ Oral corticosteroids administered from the 3rd SABA series onwards ❖ Call the emergency number if symptoms persist and signs of severity are present The administration of SABA requires the use of an inhalation chamber with a mask (for children aged 0 to 3 years) or a mouthpiece (for children aged 4 to 12 years).

text.text: Scores are used by medical teams to assess the severity of an attack.
Several scores have been validated to date, including the Asthma Severity Score, PRAM and Pulmonary Index Score, and their use depends on the centre.
The PRAM score is currently used in the Martinique pediatrics emergency department. (appendix 1) It includes several clinical warning signs that parents should look out for.

A moderate asthma attack (PRAM 4) or one with a risk of complications according to the recommendations, the following treatment should be given: ❖ Inhale four to twelve puffs of SABA adjusted to the patient's weight, every twenty minutes three times, then every one to four hours if symptoms improve.
❖ If symptoms persist after the third course, oral corticosteroids should be prescribed at a dosage appropriate for the patient's weight, not exceeding 60 mg/day of prednisolone.
❖ If symptoms persist after the third series, or if there are signs of respiratory distress or clinical severity criteria, call the emergency services.
For mild attacks (PRAM 1 to 3), with isolated coughing or mild symptoms, recommendations are not fixed and are often left to the discretion of the practitioner.
One possible treatment option is as follows: ❖ Inhale four puffs of SABA, repeating every twenty minutes if necessary.
❖ If symptoms worsen, follow the protocol for moderate or severe asthma attacks.

According to the GINA 2024 guidelines, an alternative treatment is preferred for patients aged 12 years and older: ❖ The combination of inhaled corticosteroids and formoterol would be preferred for initiating maintenance treatment and could be used during attacks in patients receiving this maintenance treatment.
❖ The maximum number of inhalations recommended before seeking emergency medical attention is height in one day.
The goal is to limit the number of treatments patients need to take and to promote patient adherence to treatment.
The first-line chronic treatments are inhaled corticosteroids (ICS).
They are administered daily and their dosage and use of the inhalation device must be reassessed regularly.
Their use reduces asthma-related mortality, the number of hospitalizations, the frequency and severity of asthma attacks.
They also improve symptom control and quality of life, and preserve respiratory function. (12) Additional treatments may be prescribed for asthma that is not controlled by ICS alone.
text.formatted: They also improve symptom control and quality of life, and preserve respiratory function. <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(12)</ref> Additional treatments may be prescribed for asthma that is not controlled by ICS alone.

text.text: ICS may be combined with long-acting bronchodilators (LABA), anticholinergics, or leukotriene antagonists (LA).

For asthma that is resistant to high doses of ICS (step 5), biotherapies may be initiated in specialist centers in accordance with recent recommendations from the French Pediatric Pulmonology and Allergology Society. (11) According to the GINA 2024 guidelines, an alternative treatment is preferred for patients aged 12 years and older, although the ICS +/-SABA option remains among the treatment options.

text.text: The management of asthma requires effective coordination between various medical and paramedical professionals.
The general practitioner plays a central role in the overall management of children with asthma, but various other healthcare professionals are needed to ensure proper follow-up.
Specialists (pulmonologists, pediatric pulmonologists, allergists) have a role to play, particularly in cases of moderate to severe asthma requiring more intensive treatment.
Pediatric emergency services are necessary when attacks are poorly controlled despite outpatient treatment.

Asthma education in hospital through the asthma school, plays a vital role in prevention and teaching children and their parents about asthma. (13) Several obstacles to the proper monitoring of asthma patients currently exist in Martinique and France.

text.text: Healthcare provision is an integral part of the factors influencing the proper care of children with asthma.
There is currently a wide variety of healthcare provision at the national level.
This heterogeneity in access to healthcare providers is illustrated by comparing healthcare provision between different departments and, on a smaller scale, between rural areas and cities.

Thanks to the government's regional observatory website (14) https://www.zotero.org/google-docs/?mHE2yc we were able to compare healthcare provision in Martinique with that in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department.

text.text: In terms of demographics, the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department had a population of 706,360 in 2023.
There are 787 general practitioners practicing in this area, 56 private pulmonologists, and 37 private pediatricians.
In comparison, Martinique had approximately 7 . 350,000 inhabitants in 2023.
There were 330 private general practitioners.
There are 6 private pulmonologists and 7 private pediatricians.

Although outpatient consultations are organized by specialists at the University of Martinique Hospital to meet demand (in pediatrics and pulmonology), access to specialist consultations is objectively lower in Martinique.

The provision of general medical care, if we compare the number of general practitioners to the number of inhabitants, is fairly similar (1 general practitioner for every 897 inhabitants in the Pyrénées-Atlantiques, compared to 1 for every 1,060 inhabitants in Martinique).
In pediatrics, parents play a fundamental role in the medical care of their children.

Among the skills they need to acquire, we will ask them to learn how to recognize an asthma attack, how to recognize the signs of a severe attack, how to administer the necessary emergency treatment by following the action plan, how to use medical devices at home, and how to alert medical personnel at the right time.
By detailing this knowledge, we can understand the importance of education and prevention in ensuring that the child and those around them are prepared in the event of an exacerbation.
In addition, the child must be quickly included in the medical discussion during consultations in order to gradually develop autonomy in their care.
All these areas of competence can only be recorded and understood through regular monitoring, consultations focused on prevention, and good coordination between healthcare professionals.
It was precisely in this context that the asthma school was invented in 1992 by the "Asthme et allergie" association in mainland France.

The University of Martinique Hospital has its own asthma school, accredited by the regional health agency since 2015, which provides therapeutic education and a prevention space for families of children with asthma.

It forms an important pillar of care for asthma patients in Martinique through awareness-raising meetings with groups of parents, as well as individualized consultations that allow for a personalized approach to care.
According to our data, there were approximately 1,600 visits to the pediatric emergency department at the University of Martinique Hospital between January 2023 and December 2023 for asthma attacks.

This represents the second most common reason for emergency room visits during this period (after fever), accounting for approximately 7% of visits and requiring hospitalization in 9.6% of cases, representing 154 hospitalizations.

A certain proportion of patients consulting for asthma attacks at the MFME pediatric emergency department did not receive appropriate treatment prior to their arrival, and a significant proportion presented with symptoms classified as mild asthma attacks (according to the PRAM classification).
Based on this assumption, we decided to initiate this study.
The main objective of this study is to evaluate the management of asthma attacks prior to consultation at the pediatric emergency department at the University of Martinique Hospital.

Secondly, we will explore data that may explain the poor management of exacerbations in asthmatic children in the pre-hospital setting, by assessing asthma control prior to the attack and describing the medical follow-up of asthmatic patients.
The secondary objective is to propose areas for improvement in the medical and paramedical management of asthmatic children in Martinique.

We conducted a prospective, descriptive, single-center, cross-sectional study including children residing in Martinique aged between 1 and 18 years old, previously diagnosed with asthma and attending the pediatric emergency department in the university hospital of Martinique due to an asthma exacerbation.
We chose a prospective study in order to increase its power, defining in advance the most relevant clinical data to be collected.
Secondly, we examined asthma control in each patient during the month preceding the crisis using the asthma control criteria set out in the GINA guidelines.
Several other data were analyzed, such as the patient's usual medical follow-up, the parents' feelings about the attack, and the current maintenance treatments.

Certain data, such as weight, treatments administered in the emergency department, and parameters on admission to the emergency department, were retrieved retrospectively in order to refine our analyses.
For patient recruitment, questionnaires (Supplementary 1) were distributed in the pediatric emergency department in the university hospital of Martinique to parents consulting for asthma attacks.

We took advantage of the long duration of care in the emergency department, due to the frequent need for short-acting bronchodilator inhalation, to distribute the questionnaires to parents accompanying their children, thereby theoretically increasing the response rate among parents.
The questionnaire was distributed by the physicians in charge of the asthmatic patient once the clinical evaluation had been completed and treatment had begun.

This questionnaire has four different sections: factors motivating the visit to the emergency room, asthma control criteria, asthma history, parents' knowledge, and treatments administered at home for the current attack.
The questionnaire takes approximately 15-20 minutes to complete and contains 34 items to check off.
The questionnaires were distributed over a four-month period from July 1 to November 1, 2024.
The study focused on evaluating pre-hospital care for asthma attacks in children aged 1 to 18 years, and we included all asthma attacks in patients with known asthma in this age group.
Patients had to meet the clinical and paraclinical criteria for diagnosing an asthma attack, such as dyspnea, wheezing, coughing, and auscultatory wheezing.
These attack criteria were not clearly established or imposed on the practitioner.
We therefore implicitly accepted each diagnosis once it had been made.

The practitioners who could administer the questionnaires were as follows: senior physicians, residents specializing in general medicine, pediatrics, and emergency medicine working in the pediatric emergency department.
We excluded any child presenting their first asthma attack (previously undiagnosed asthma).
Patients not residing in Martinique.
Patients with a differential diagnosis of dyspnea (such as pneumonia).
Patients not accompanied by one of their parents.
We also excluded patients under one year of age (to avoid selection bias related to the bronchiolitis epidemic prevalent during the winter) and patients over 18 years of age.
Questionnaires with less than 50% of questions answered were excluded.
For the therapeutic assessment of asthma attacks in the pre-hospital setting, there are numerous recommendations, and these are not entirely consistent across countries and scientific committees.

We referred to the tools used in the pediatric emergency department in the university hospital of Martinique to achieve local and regional consistency in the use of emergency treatments for asthma patients.

We therefore relied on the recommendations of the French university hospital Trousseau in Paris, particularly its emergency action plan, to determine the doses of short-acting bronchodilators to be administered based on the child's weight. (15) We also used this action plan to determine the time interval between doses of SABA and the timing of oral corticosteroid administration if signs of respiratory distress persisted.

For the asthma control criterion, we referred to the GINA 2024 recommendations.
Asthma control is divided into 3 subgroups based on the symptoms reported by the children during the month preceding the asthma attack.

❖ Uncontrolled (if more than 2 items are checked).

The items in question are as follows: use of SABA more than once a week for children under 6 years of age and more than twice a week for children over 6 years of age; a nighttime cough; asthma-related activity limitations; and daytime symptoms more than twice a week.
This assessment of asthma control will help identify children with poor asthma control who may require an adjustment to their maintenance therapy.
Since it has been proven that proper adjustment of maintenance therapy for asthma reduces the risk of asthma exacerbations (in terms of frequency, not severity). ( 16)

text.text: For the criteria for optimal medical care of patients with asthma, we referred to GINA 2024, which defines several criteria for effective disease management: 12 .
○ A follow-up visit for asthma within 6 months or 1 year if there are no changes to the treatment regimen, depending on the severity of the asthma.

Note that severity is defined by the intensity of treatment required to control the asthma, which is why it is necessary to continually reassess maintenance therapy to determine the minimum effective doses.
○ If a change is made to the maintenance therapy, a follow-up visit must be scheduled in 3 months.
○ Multidisciplinary care is not recommended given the risk that conflicting messages may lead to a disruption in care.
Optimal coordination among the various stakeholders is therefore essential.

○ A child with asthma who is over 6 years old is eligible for a pulmonary function testing, which is necessary to assess asthma control in these patients (and thus to adjust their long-term treatment). (17) ○ A pulmonary function test should be performed at least once a year if maintenance therapy is necessary to control asthma.

The population is described in terms of its count and percentage for qualitative and categorical variables, and in terms of the median and the 25th and 75th percentiles for quantitative variables.
Comparative analyses to calculate the p-value were performed using the Mann-Whitney test for continuous quantitative variables and the chi-square test for binary variables.
A p-value less than 0.01 was considered statistically significant.

The size effect was calculated for continuous quantitative variables using a standardized mean difference and for binary variables using the Mahalanobis distance, with a 95% confidence interval calculated.
These analyses, as well as the creation of the figures, were performed using custom Python code (Python 3.9).
The p-value was calculated using the scipy package.
The effect size was calculated using the effectsize package (https://github.com/nbashir97/effectsize).

This study was conducted as a cross-sectional, prospective study; the response rate to the questionnaire was good, allowing for the enrollment of 175 patients out of the 181 questionnaires distributed during the period from July through the end of October 2024.
The primary objective of the study was to describe and evaluate the management of asthma attacks in children aged 1 to 18 years prior to presentation at the pediatric emergency department.

One of the reasons for conducting this study is the high prevalence of asthma in Martinique, as well as the significant challenges in managing this chronic disease, due to the variety of factors required for its optimal clinical control.
The vast majority of patients included in the study were between 1 and 11 years old, accounting for 86.3% of the study population.
Adolescents aged 12 to 18 accounted for 13.7% of the study population.

Adolescents are a difficult-to-treat population; they rarely seek medical care and tend to present to the emergency department only when their asthma has actually deteriorated significantly, with severe asthma attack criteria, thereby increasing the risk of serious respiratory decompensation and admission to the intensive care unit. text.text: Several factors come into play in the proper management of an asthma attack-both from a therapeutic standpoint, involving various treatments, and from a behavioral standpoint, particularly the ability to recognize signs of respiratory distress, the ability to alert others, and the appropriate waiting time before seeking emergency care.
This multifactorial nature has made it difficult to accurately assess the management of asthma attacks in the prehospital setting.
To evaluate it comprehensively, we developed a score ranging from 0 to 10 that combines several management criteria we consider important.
To develop this score, we ranked the priority interventions for the proper management of asthma attacks in children.
We felt that the most important intervention was SABA treatment at home (3 points).
The results are detailed in Table 2.

text.text: Slightly more than 1 in 10 patients (11.1%) did not receive a SABA before their emergency department visit.
Among the 88.9% who took SABA, 52.5% administered at least 3 doses. (2 points) Furthermore, 68% of patients had a valid prescription for Ventolin or Ventolin at home.
This finding highlights the limitations of attributing poor prehospital therapeutic management solely to parents; a lack of follow-up and foresight can affect asthma attacks.
Management of an asthma attack involves two distinct approaches depending on the severity and tolerance of the attack.
If symptoms are mild, it may be recommended to space out SABA doses by 4 hours and repeat as needed until symptoms improve.
If the attack worsens or is moderate or severe from the outset, administering SABA every 20 minutes for 1 hour is indicated.
The questionnaire did not distinguish between these two situations and could therefore be confusing.
We decided to award only one point for this parameter, and 66.2% of patients maintained an interval of <1 hour between Ventolin doses.

Special attention could be given to the under-6 age group, particularly in strengthening prevention measures.
There is currently significant room for improvement in the prehospital management of asthma attacks.
Focusing our efforts on this phase of asthma could reduce the morbidity associated with the disease.

Ultimately, we could significantly reduce the psychological impact on patients and improve their quality of life by decreasing the number of emergency department visits, as well as by reducing anxiety related to asthma attacks through a better understanding of the disease.
One of the goals is to reduce the social impact of the disease, such as school absenteeism.
The number of visits to pediatric emergency departments could decrease, which would improve the quality of care for other patients by reducing the workload of healthcare providers.

Healthcare costs related to asthma are currently substantial, and a shift toward prevention-focused care could not only improve the quality of patient care but also reduce public spending in the long term. (20) All of these factors must be taken into account to improve asthma care in Martinique.

It is possible that many of the reported follow-up visits were solely for the purpose of completing the individualized welcome plan required by elementary and middle schools.

Slightly fewer than one in two patients therefore showed signs of poor asthma control in the previous month; these warning signs-such as a loss of control over asthma symptoms-should, in theory, alert the family and lead to a medical consultation for reevaluation.
One of the factors complicating this analysis is the inclusion of patients currently under follow-up for poorly controlled asthma who may be in the therapeutic adjustment phase.
We investigated whether there might be a link between the degree of asthma control and the potential severity of an asthma attack in our population.

We observed that the number of patients treated in the emergency resuscitation unit was higher among well-controlled patients, but that the number of children transferred to the intensive care unit was higher among partially or poorly controlled patients (3 in total).
Given the small proportion of patients requiring intensive care (3 out of 174), it is difficult to draw conclusions about a causal relationship.
Some studies have found a causal link between poor clinical control and morbidity and mortality associated with asthma attacks.

(23) In this study, conducted in primary care settings, 3,431 patients were included; of these, 26% had good asthma control, 41.3% had moderate control, and 32.7% had poor asthma control.

text.text: This is an older but compelling study, with a different research approach (recruitment from primary care settings).
Despite this, the percentage of patients with well-controlled asthma in our study is higher.

Although 13 years have passed since that study, and setting aside any differences and biases, we can assume that asthma control is slightly better today in Martinique than it was in mainland France in 2009.

According to current GINA recommendations, a child with asthma should be monitored by a primary care physician without the need for a specialist consultation if the asthma is well-controlled and of mild severity.
It should be noted that the definition of asthma severity depends on the intensity of the maintenance therapy prescribed to control symptoms.
Referral to a specialist should therefore be considered if asthma control proves 27.
difficult and requires an increase in dosage or a change in the type of maintenance therapy, classifying the asthma as moderate to severe.
In our study, 22.3% of parents reported that their child's asthma was not being medically managed.
This represents nearly 1 in 5 children who visit the emergency room.
Among children receiving medical care, 54.8% of those under 6 years of age are managed by their primary care physician, and 16.7% of them are seen by a pediatrician.
The transition from pediatric care to primary care appears to occur around age 6, since 70.3% of children over 6 years of age receive asthma care from their general practitioner.
Medical management of asthma by an allergist is around 25% among patients over 6 years of age, compared to nearly 12% managed by a pulmonologist.
There may be a bias in these data, since one pulmonologist (out of the six private-practice pulmonologists in Martinique) specializes in allergology.
As described in the introduction, the availability of care in Martinique is limited in the private-practice specialties of pulmonology, allergology, and pediatrics.
General practitioners therefore play a central role in the care of patients with asthma, regardless of their age.

Asthma is a highly prevalent disease affecting populations worldwide.
There are numerous studies and medical articles on the subject, which have enabled the gradual evolution of medical recommendations aimed at improving the management of asthma.
Unfortunately, changes in expert recommendations can sometimes occur more rapidly than changes in medical practice. (30).

Standardizing practices requires the use of the same guidelines and the same tools.

A collaborative effort could be undertaken with the adult pulmonology department, pediatric pulmonologists, referring general practitioners, and specialized nurses to develop uniform action plans and individualized care plans throughout Martinique.
And perhaps a digital platform could be created to make these documents available.
A computer-based tool to assist physicians in decision-making-particularly regarding the initiation or adjustment of treatment-could also be developed.

Increasing the recruitment of physicians specializing in pulmonology and pediatric pulmonology could lighten the already very diverse workload of general practitioners and help ensure better patient care.

To achieve this, the region must be attractive to these specialists; however, raising awareness of the challenges involved in managing asthma and highlighting current initiatives to develop and improve the healthcare network could potentially attract more than a few of them.

Helping to develop primary care clinics-which serve as a screening mechanism before patients seek emergency care-and establishing common, standardized protocols with emergency services in the event of a crisis could be another area of focus.
The lack of reimbursement for therapeutic education consultations-which are generally lengthy-does not encourage preventive care in private practice.
A specific fee schedule tailored to therapeutic education consultations could be one of the tools used to change practices in private practice.

text.text: Pulmonary function testing is the cornerstone of paraclinical evaluations in children with asthma.
It allows for an accurate assessment of the patient's lung function and is useful for monitoring, adjusting treatment, and evaluating the impact on respiratory function over time.
Given the clinical heterogeneity of asthma, its use can accurately assess a patient's respiratory function and guide the clinician in managing the patient's care.
In our study, 14.3% of children over the age of 6 had access to pulmonary function testing.

A study could be proposed among primary care physicians to assess their attitudes toward the use of pulmonary function testing, as well as their self-assessment of their ability to interpret the results and the barriers to prescribing it (difficulties in access, lack of familiarity, and lack of training).
In our study, only 4 children had a peak flow meter at home, and 13 caregivers believed they knew how to use it.
The EDELMA study, conducted in 2018 at the CHUM's asthma school, found that 4 of the 108 children included in the study reported that they had mastered the device.
To date, the use of peak flow measurement is recommended primarily for patients with mild asthma symptoms or those who are unable to assess the severity of their attack.

This tool provides a visual assessment of the breathing difficulty associated with the attack and may allow for faster initiation of treatment, thereby potentially increasing the effectiveness of emergency therapy.
A prospective study conducted in 2024 demonstrates the usefulness of peak flow measurement in assessing how children with asthma perceive their respiratory limitations.

In this case, three exhalations should be taken each time the device is used, and the highest value should be recorded.
Its use can aid in the diagnosis of asthma (if clinical findings are consistent with asthma and spirometry is not available); normal DEP values do not rule out a diagnosis of asthma.
Improvements in peak flow readings are generally observed within 3 months of starting inhaled corticosteroids.
To ensure an adequate response to treatment, patients are asked to take two measurements per day for 2 weeks and record them in a chart.

One potential area for improvement could be the use of the peak expiratory flow in pediatric emergency departments to assess severity upon arrival, as well as to guide the decision to discharge patients treated in the emergency department or to help determine whether hospitalization is indicated.
To achieve this, standardizing its use and providing training for medical and paramedical staff is crucial.
A pulse oximeter is a noninvasive, easy-to-use device that measures blood oxygen saturation.
It is widely used in medical and paramedical settings, but its usefulness in the homes of patients with asthma has not yet been proven..

Although oxygen saturation-when it is 94% or lower-is one of the criteria used to assess the severity of an asthma attack, there are several limitations to the optimal use of a pulse oximeter: ➔ poor perfusion at the measurement site.
➔ irregular pulse.
➔ skin color and thickness.
➔ incorrect positioning.
➔ the use of adult pulse oximeters on children.
➔ devices have a margin of error of +/-4% for saturation levels between 70% and 100%.
➔ decreased oxygen saturation in children after taking SABA.
➔ interpreting saturation outside the context of a crisis.

All of these confounding factors, when considered in isolation, can lead to a misinterpretation of the severity of an asthma attack and, consequently, increase anxiety among caregivers and lead to more frequent visits to the emergency room.
It can be assumed that appropriate use of the device at home by patients must be accompanied by a good understanding of the instructions for use and a solid knowledge of asthma.

One area for improvement would be the use and evaluation of available digital tools.
Currently, several apps exist to help manage asthma (and are available on smartphones).
For example, the "findair" app helps track medication use and alerts users to poor asthma control if rescue medication is used too frequently.
"Smart Asthma" allows users to monitor lung function using a peak flow meter.
Some peak flow meters are equipped with Bluetooth or connect directly to a smartphone, allowing users to enter readings directly and facilitating monitoring.
The "effic'asthme" app was developed by the AP-HP in 2019.
It is a virtual asthma attack simulation app that allows parents and patients to practice responding appropriately to an asthma attack.
In our study, a small proportion of parents had heard of the asthma school, and only 15.3% had taken their child for a consultation there.

A study conducted at the CHUM from January through December 2018 (the EDELMA study) documented significant changes in habits as well as positive changes in medication adherence and healthcare utilization-particularly visits to the emergency department-among patients enrolled in the asthma education program.
Awareness and prevention sessions were held weekly at the CHUM, and individual consultations were offered to promote treatment adherence.

During these sessions, several topics were addressed, such as empowering the child, recognizing the signs of an asthma attack, communication between children and parents, inhalation techniques, and various other prevention strategies.
This opportunity for discussion proved to be essential.

Among the children attending the asthma clinic in this study, only 2.4% were referred by their primary care physician (66% were referred from the emergency department and 27% from the inpatient unit).
This trend appears to be reversing at present, which may point to a lack of communication in the emergency department.

A medical thesis conducted in Martinique in 2015, which described the practices of general practitioners in the region, found that 83% of the physicians surveyed were familiar with the "Asthma School."
Rather than a lack of knowledge, a lack of familiarity with its use in daily practice may be suspected.
A questionnaire was distributed to each physician (240 practitioners), and the response rate was 37%.
The objective of the study was to evaluate the management of asthma by general practitioners in the territory and to compare it to the guidelines that had been in effect for 10 years at that time.

In this thesis, 82% of the physicians surveyed wanted to be able to delegate therapeutic education to a facility or a trained professional, while 72% felt they were not providing enough therapeutic education.
However, therapeutic education is key to asthma management and is central to the work carried out by the asthma school.
Currently, the asthma school limits its activities to pediatrics, but the expansion of this program (in terms of staff and resources) could facilitate the extension of its services to adults.
A better understanding of the disease in adults could thus have a beneficial effect on the care of children.
Currently, a project to assess homes for irritants and allergens is being developed in collaboration with the Asthma School.
This type of field intervention could facilitate research, concrete action, and awareness-raising among families.

The heterogeneity of (mild) recommendations-but especially of medical practices-introduces a bias in the evaluation of prehospital care for patients.
A 2015 doctoral thesis conducted in Martinique illustrated this diversity in asthma management in primary care.
The study's assessment of prehospital care is therefore naturally influenced not only by patients' understanding but also by medical practices that are sometimes inconsistent.
This inconsistency in the messages conveyed to patients can sometimes reduce adherence to or understanding of medical advice, especially among patients receiving multidisciplinary care.
Standardizing medical advice is a priority not only to facilitate the management of asthma attacks but also to control asthma in children.

By choosing to recruit patients in the emergency department, one may be exposed to a population of children with asthma who are predominantly poorly controlled or poorly managed medically, and may underestimate the number of well-controlled and well-managed patients in the general population.
Indeed, a close link between poor asthma control and the risk of asthma exacerbations is well known and has been described.
(29) A follow-up study conducted in primary care could, in the future, supplement our data and help identify specific areas for improvement in patient care.
(31) Differences in care and a lack of updated knowledge can affect all medical specialties, particularly within a single emergency department.
(32) Regular continuing education for physicians and the standardization of care based on guidelines could ultimately improve asthma management in Martinique.

Several types of continuing education tools aimed at healthcare providers (residents, general practitioners, and specialized nurses) can be-and are being-developed in the form of seminars and online training courses, for example.
